entries.meaning: Daśaratha attained the fruit of both life and death: while alive he beheld Rāma’s moonlike face, and by dying in separation from Rāma perfected his end; his stainless fame spread through countless worlds. All the grief-stricken queens wept, recounting his beauty, character, strength, and splendor, lamenting in many ways and repeatedly falling to the ground. Distraught servants wailed, and residents mourned in every home: “Today the sun of the solar line has set—the boundary of righteousness, treasury of virtue, beauty, and dignity.” Everyone hurled abuse at Kaikeyī, who had made the world sightless. As the night passed in this lamentation, all the learned great sages arrived. Vasiṣṭha then spoke many timely teachings and histories; by the light of his knowledge he checked everyone’s grief.

They placed the king’s body in a vessel filled with oil. Vasiṣṭha summoned messengers and said: “Hurry swiftly to Bharata, but tell no one any news of the king. Say only that the guru has summoned both brothers and sent for them.” Hearing the sage’s command, the couriers rushed off, moving so swiftly that they shamed fine horses. From the time calamity began in Ayodhyā, ill omens had come to Bharata. At night he saw terrifying dreams, and on waking imagined millions of bitter outcomes. He fed brahmins, gave gifts daily, and performed Śiva’s ablution in many ways; propitiating Maheśa, he prayed inwardly for the welfare of mother, father, family, and brothers. As Bharata worried in this way, the couriers arrived. Hearing the guru’s direction, he invoked Gaṇeśa and departed.

They drove horses at the wind’s speed, crossing rivers, rugged mountains, and forests. Great anxiety filled Bharata’s heart and nothing pleased him; inwardly he wished he could fly. A single instant passed like a year as he approached the city. Inauspicious signs appeared when he entered: crows called harshly from bad fields and riverbanks, and donkeys and jackals cried against him; each sound pierced Bharata’s mind. Ponds, rivers, woods, and gardens had lost their beauty, while the city appeared especially frightening. Birds, deer, horses, and elephants were not to be seen, wasted by the grievous sickness of separation from Rāma. The city’s women and men were utterly miserable, as though every one had lost every possession. Citizens met him but said nothing; they offered salutation with sighs and moved on. Bharata could not ask of their welfare, for fear and sorrow filled his mind.

Markets and roads could scarcely be looked upon; it seemed a wildfire had seized the city in all ten directions. Hearing that her son had come, Kaikeyī’s daughter rejoiced, like moonlight to the solar dynasty’s lotus. She prepared the welcoming lamp, happily ran out, met him at the doorway, and brought him inside. Bharata saw the household grieving as though a lotus grove had been struck by frost. Kaikeyī, by contrast, rejoiced like a huntress delighted after setting a forest fire. Seeing her son anxious, she suppressed her feelings and asked after the welfare of her parental home. Bharata reported that all were well and asked in turn about his own family: “Tell me, where is father? Where are all the mothers? Where are Sītā, Rāma, and my dear brother Lakṣmaṇa?” Hearing her son’s affectionate words, the sinful woman feigned tears and spoke words that pierced Bharata’s ears and mind like a spear.

Kaikeyī said: “Son, I arranged the entire affair. Mantharā, whom I wisely made my helper, assisted me. Fate spoiled only a small part of the business: the king set foot in Indra’s city.” Hearing this, Bharata became helpless with grief, like an elephant calf terrified by a lion’s roar. Crying “Father! Father! Ah, father!” he fell heavily upon the ground. “As you departed I did not obtain sight of you, father, nor did you entrust me to Rāma!” Regaining some composure he rose and asked his mother the cause of his father’s death. In reply Kaikeyī pierced the wound as though administering poison afterward: from the beginning she happily related all her crooked, cruel actions as her own achievement. When Bharata heard that Rāma had gone to the forest, even his father’s death vanished from his awareness. Recognizing himself as the cause, he stood stunned and silent.

Seeing her son distraught, Kaikeyī tried to console him, like putting salt upon a burn: “Son, the king is not fit to be mourned. He enlarged his store of merit and fame and enjoyed its fruit; in life he gained every reward of birth, and at the end he went to the immortal lord’s abode. Understanding this, set grief aside and rule the city together with the assembly.” Hearing her, the prince recoiled as if a glowing coal had touched a ripened wound. Holding himself steady and drawing a deep breath, he replied: “Sinful woman, you have destroyed the lineage in every way. If such evil intent possessed you, why did you not kill me at birth? You raised and watered a tree only to cut it down, and continually bailed away the very water in which the fish lives. Daśaratha was born in the swan dynasty, Janaka is Rāma’s father-in-law, and Lakṣmaṇa is my brother; yet you became my mother—against Fate there is no power.”

Bharata continued: “When you fixed this wicked counsel in your heart, why did the heart not break into pieces? Why did your mind feel no pain in asking the boons, your tongue not rot, and worms not fill your mouth? How did the king place trust in you? At the hour of death, Fate stole his judgment. Not even Fate has understood a woman’s heart, a mine of deceit, sin, and faults. How could the guileless, virtuous king devoted to righteousness know such a disposition? What living creature exists to whom Raghunātha is not dearer than life? Even Rāma became your bitter enemy—who are you? Tell me truly! Whatever laugh you possess, laugh it now, blackening your face; then rise and go hide from my sight. Fate has revealed me from the heart as an enemy of Rāma. Who is a sinner equal to me? It is useless to say anything more to you.”

Hearing of his mother’s crookedness, Śatrughna burned with rage through every limb and could do nothing to contain it. Just then the hunchback Mantharā appeared, arrayed in various garments and ornaments. Seeing her, Lakṣmaṇa’s younger brother filled with fury like a blazing fire receiving an oblation of ghee. He sprang forward, aimed a kick at her hump, and struck. She fell face-first upon the ground screaming; her hump broke, her skull split, her teeth were smashed, and blood streamed from her mouth. She cried, “Ah Fate! What have I ruined? I did good and have received its reward!” Hearing her, Ripuhana saw her wicked from nail to crown and began dragging her by the hair. Compassionate Bharata made him release her, and the two brothers went to Kauśalyā. She wore soiled clothes and was pale, distraught, emaciated, and burdened with grief—like a fine golden wish-fulfilling vine struck by frost.

Seeing Bharata, his mother rose and rushed toward him, but swooned and fell to the ground midway. At the sight Bharata became profoundly distraught, fell at her feet, and forgot the condition of his own body. “Mother, show me where father is! Where are Sītā, Rāma, and my brother Lakṣmaṇa? Why was Kaikeyī born into the world? If born, why was she not barren? She bore me, a stain upon the lineage, vessel of infamy, betrayer of those dear to me. Who in the three worlds is as unfortunate as I, mother, upon whom such a fate has fallen? Father is in heaven, Raghubara the banner of his line in the forest, and I alone am the cause of every disaster. Shame upon me! I have become a forest fire to the bamboo grove of my lineage, heir to intolerable burning, grief, and blame.” Hearing Bharata’s gentle words, his mother gradually recovered, lifted him, embraced him to her heart, and shed tears.

In her guileless nature Kauśalyā drew Bharata to her heart with the deepest affection, as though Rāma had returned. She then embraced Lakṣmaṇa’s younger brother; grief and love could not fit within her heart. Seeing her disposition, everyone said, “Why should she not be Rāma’s mother?” Seating Bharata in her lap, she wiped away his tears and spoke tenderly: “Even now, dear child, take courage for my sake; understand this hostile time and relinquish grief. Do not harbor loss or shame in your heart—know the course of time and action to be beyond imagining. Do not blame anyone, son; Fate has opposed me in every way. Who knows what more it intends, when it kept me alive through even this suffering? At his father’s command Raghubīra abandoned ornaments and clothes, son; feeling neither astonishment nor elation in his heart, he put on garments of bark.”
